You are reverse-engineering a C++ library PURELY AS A BLACK BOX by running a compiled binary.

BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test16_executable
Its C++ driver source is (library source is NOT available - do not look for it):

  int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
      if (argc < 2) return 1;
      std::string url = argv[1];
      std::cout << url_parser::URL::is_valid_url(url) << std::endl;       // LINE 1
      url_parser::URL parser(url);
      std::cout << url_parser::is_scheme_valid(parser.scheme()) << std::endl;  // LINE 2
      std::cout << url_parser::is_host_valid(parser.host()) << std::endl;      // LINE 3
      std::cout << url_parser::is_port_valid(parser.port()) << std::endl;      // LINE 4
      auto path_segments = url_parser::split_path(parser.path());
      std::cout << path_segments.size() << std::endl;                          // LINE 5
      for (const auto& segment : path_segments) std::cout << segment << std::endl;  // LINES 6+
      return 0;
  }

So each run gives you exactly 5 numbers + the path segments. Lines 1-4 are bools printed as 1/0.

KNOWN INTERFACE (from the binary's symbol table - this is all you get):
  namespace url_parser {
    std::string url_decode(const std::string&);
    std::string url_encode(const std::string&);
    std::vector<std::string> split_path(const std::string&);
    bool is_scheme_valid(const std::string&);
    bool is_host_valid(const std::string&);
    bool is_port_valid(int);                 // NOTE: port is an int
    static bool URL::is_valid_url(const std::string&);
    class URL {
      URL(); URL(const std::string&);
      void parse(const std::string&);
      std::string scheme() const; std::string userinfo() const; std::string host() const;
      int port() const; std::string path() const; std::string query() const;
      std::string fragment() const; std::string authority() const;
      bool has_scheme/has_authority/has_userinfo/has_host/has_port/has_path/has_query/has_fragment() const;
      bool is_valid() const;
      ... setters, normalize(), normalize_case(), normalize_path(), normalize_query(), to_string(), operator==
    };
    // internal statics: trim(const std::string&), to_lower(const std::string&),
    //                   is_hex(char), hex_to_char(char)
    // to_lower is implemented as std::transform with a lambda taking (unsigned char)
  }

PROBE HARNESS - use this pattern (handles quoting safely):
  BIN=/workspace/dataset/test16_executable
  probe() { printf '%s => ' "$(printf '%q' "$1")"; "$BIN" "$1" 2>&1 | tr '\n' '|'; printf ' (exit %s)\n' "${PIPESTATUS[0]}"; }
  probe 'http://example.com'
  probe $'http://a\tb'        # use $'...' for control chars / tabs / newlines
  probe "$(printf 'http://a\xc3\xa9')"   # for high bytes / UTF-8

You may run HUNDREDS of probes - do it in batches inside one bash call using loops. Be exhaustive and systematic:
sweep single characters, boundary lengths, every ASCII code 0..127 where relevant, high bytes 128..255,
empty strings, and combinations. Isolate one variable at a time.

ESTABLISHED FACTS (already confirmed, do not re-derive, but you MAY correct them if you find contradictions):
  ''                              => 0 0 0 0 0
  'http://example.com'            => 1 1 1 0 0
  'https://localhost:8080'        => 1 1 1 1 0
  'http://example.com/a/b/c'      => 1 1 1 0 3 [a,b,c]
  'http://example.com/a/b/c/'     => 1 1 1 0 3 [a,b,c]
  'http://example.com//a//b'      => 1 1 1 0 2 [a,b]      (empty segments dropped)
  'http://example.com/'           => 1 1 1 0 0
  'example.com'                   => 1 0 0 0 1 [example.com]   (no '://' => whole string is path)
  'http://example.com:0'          => 1 1 1 1 0   (port 0 IS valid => absent port must be a sentinel like -1)
  'http://example.com:65535'      => 1 1 1 1 0
  'http://example.com:65536'      => 1 1 1 0 0
  'http://example.com:-1'         => 1 1 1 0 0
  'http://example.com:abc'        => 1 1 1 0 0
  'http://example.com:'           => 1 1 1 0 0
  'http://example.com:80abc'      => 1 1 1 1 0   (looks like std::stoi: leading digits, trailing junk ignored)
  'HTTP://EXAMPLE.COM/A/B'        => 1 1 1 0 2 [A,B]  (NO case normalization in parse)
  '://example.com'                => 1 0 1 0 0   (scheme='' invalid, host='example.com')
  'http:/example.com'             => 1 0 0 0 2 [http:,example.com]
  'http://'                       => 0 1 0 0 0
  'http:///a/b'                   => 1 1 0 0 2 [a,b]
  'http://:8080'                  => 0 1 0 1 0
  'http://@example.com'           => 1 1 1 0 0   (userinfo split on '@')
  'http://example.com?a=/b/c'     => 1 1 1 0 0   (query stripped before path)
  'http://example.com#/x/y'       => 1 1 1 0 0   (fragment stripped before path)
  'http://example.com/a%20b/c%2Fd'=> 1 1 1 0 2 [a%20b,c%2Fd]  (split_path does NOT url-decode)
  'http://example.com/./../a'     => 1 1 1 0 3 [.,..,a]       (no dot-segment removal)
  'http://exa_mple.com'           => 1 1 0 0 0   (underscore => host INVALID)
  'http://-example.com'           => 1 1 1 0 0   (leading hyphen => host VALID)
  'http://example..com'           => 1 1 1 0 0   (empty label => host VALID)
  'http://[::1]:8080/x'           => 1 1 1 0 1 [x]  (!! port INVALID but host VALID - investigate)
  'http://[::1]/x'                => 1 1 1 0 1 [x]
  'http://ex ample.com'           => 1 1 0 0 0
  ':'                             => 1 0 0 0 1 [:]
  '://'                           => 0 0 0 0 0

A LEADING HYPOTHESIS for line 1 (is_valid_url), which you should test hard if it is in your scope:
  is_valid_url(u) == (!host.empty() || !path.empty())  after parsing


=== YOUR ASSIGNMENT: URL::parse decomposition ===

Determine EXACTLY how parse() decomposes the input string into scheme / userinfo / host / port / path / query / fragment.
You can only observe the 5 output lines, so design experiments that disambiguate. Techniques:
 - Put a known-valid vs known-invalid marker in a component to read its content off lines 2/3/4.
 - Line 5 + segments leak the ENTIRE path string, so you can read path() almost directly. Exploit this heavily:
   e.g. probe 'X' and look at the segments to see what fell through to path.
 - Determine the ORDER of splitting: is fragment removed before query? is query removed before path? Where does the
   authority end (first '/' vs first of '/','?','#')? Is scheme found via find("://")? first or last occurrence?
 - Where is userinfo split - first '@' or last '@' in authority? Does '@' after a '/' matter?
 - How is the port split from the host - find(':') vs rfind(':')? Is there IPv6 '[...]' special-casing?
   Resolve the 'http://[::1]:8080/x' anomaly definitively: what exactly are host() and port() there?
 - What happens with multiple '://', multiple '?', multiple '#', ':' inside path/query/fragment?
 - Is the input trimmed of whitespace first (there is an internal trim())? Which characters does trim strip?
 - Does parse lowercase anything? (facts say no, confirm)
 - Does the path keep its leading '/'? Does an empty path stay empty or become '/'?
Report the full parsing algorithm as ordered steps.

Run as many probes as it takes (hundreds is fine, batch them in loops). Do NOT stop at a plausible rule - push until every boundary is pinned by an actual observed probe result. Then report the rule so precisely that someone can implement it in Rust without ever running the binary. If you find that one of the ESTABLISHED FACTS is wrong, say so in correctionsToEstablishedFacts.

content.text: ~11,000 fuzz cases against a reference model, zero mismatches. Here's the pinned algorithm.

input.dimension: URL::parse decomposition (scheme / userinfo / host / port / path / query / fragment)

evidence.why: Fragment is removed from the WHOLE input BEFORE scheme detection. fragment="tp://x/y", remainder "ht" has no "://" so scheme/host stay empty and path=="ht". Proves step 1 precedes step 3.
Same for query: '?' is stripped before the "://" search.
Leading '#' makes the entire rest a fragment; nothing is left to parse, so line1=0.
'#' cuts before "://" even when it is inside what looks like the scheme.
FIRST "://" wins: scheme="http" (valid), rest="x://y/z", authority="x:" (host="x" valid, port string "" -> -1 -> line4=0), path="//y/z". rfind would have given scheme="http://x" (invalid).
Scheme is s[..find("://")] verbatim including ':' -> "ht:tp" invalid, yet the authority IS still parsed (host="x"). Rules out a 'scheme = up to first colon, then require //' implementation.
Scheme is taken from index 0 even when it contains '/': scheme="/a" invalid, host="b", path="/c".
FIRST '#' (find, not rfind). rfind would leave path="/b#c/d" -> 2 segments [b#c, d].
FIRST '?' (find, not rfind). rfind would give 2 segments [b?c, d].
FIRST '@': userinfo="u1", host="u2@h" which contains an invalid host byte '@' -> line3=0. Last-'@' semantics would give host="h" -> line3=1.
First '@' => hostport="h1@h2:99" => host="h1@h2" (invalid) but port=99 (valid). Pins both 'first @' and 'port split happens after userinfo removal'.
userinfo="a:8080" is removed FIRST, so the ':' inside it is not a port separator; hostport="example.com" has no ':' => port=-1 => line4=0.
The '@' search is confined to the authority (text before the first '/'); an '@' in the path is inert.
Definitive resolution of the IPv6 anomaly: first ':' splits hostport="[::1]:8080" into host="[" (valid byte) and port string ":1]:8080" (stoi throws) -> port=-1. No bracket special-casing.
host="[_" (bytes before the first ':') contains '_' -> invalid, confirming host really is the prefix up to the first ':' and not the whole bracketed literal.
No ':' inside the brackets => host="[a]" is valid and port=80 parses. '[' and ']' are ordinary accepted host bytes.
Bracket order is irrelevant; nothing bracket-aware exists.
KEY PROOF that path keeps its leading '/': scheme="a", rest="/", authority="" (host empty, line3=0) and yet line1=1, which under is_valid_url=(host||path) requires path=="/" non-empty.
Companion to the above: rest=="" so authority="" and path=="" -> line1=0. Distinguishes path="/" from path="".
No '/' after the authority => path is EMPTY, not "example.com" (which would print 1 segment).
rest="/b", first '/' at index 0 => authority="" (host empty), path="/b".
rest="//a": authority="", path="//a" -> empty segment dropped.
NO trim: scheme==" http" is invalid although is_scheme_valid("http")==1.
NO trim: host=="a.com " invalid although is_host_valid("a.com")==1.
NO trim: trailing space kept inside the path segment.
od -c confirms every control byte survives verbatim in path; trim() is never applied by parse.
port==0 (valid) => std::stoi is base 10; hex auto-detection would give 65536 -> line4=0.
stoi skips leading isspace bytes and accepts an explicit '+' sign.
Trailing junk ignored (values 1, 1, 8) — classic std::stoi.
Zero digits consumed => std::invalid_argument => port sentinel -1.
std::out_of_range => -1 (not 0, which would have been valid, and not a clamp).
First ':' splits, port string "1:2" -> stoi = 1 (valid). rfind would give host="a:1" (invalid) + port 2.
No percent-decoding during parse: host stays "example%2Ecom" ('%' invalid).
Path is not decoded, so an encoded slash does not create a new segment.
No "://" => no scheme, no authority; path is the entire string "//a/b".
"scheme:" without "//" is not recognized; whole string becomes the path.
Empty userinfo and empty host are both representable; host=="" is the only reason line3 goes to 0 in the middle case.

evidence.input: fuzz: 6 seeds x ~1200 token-assembled inputs (plus 5 more seeds on shorter/longer variants), ~11000 total
evidence.output: total 1207 mismatch 0 (x6), all five lines + every segment string byte-identical to the reference model
evidence.why: End-to-end validation of the complete algorithm above, including the '://', '@@', '::', tab, high-byte and huge-number token cases.

uncertainties: The relative order of the fragment split and the query split is NOT observable through this driver (only scheme/host/port/path are printed, and both orders yield path == input[..min(first '#', first '?')]). I report '#' first, then '?', which is the conventional implementation; if the library actually splits '?' first then query() would swallow the '#...' tail while fragment() stayed empty. Nothing about lines 1-5 changes either way.

The port sentinel is only known to be a value for which is_port_valid() is false (i.e. <0 or >65535). -1 is the natural choice and is consistent with everything observed, but an absent port and an unparseable port string are indistinguishable from outside, as are -1 and, say, -2 or 70000.

std::stoi's exact whitespace set was verified for ' ', '\t', '\n', '\r', '\v', '\f' (all skipped). Locale-dependent behavior for other bytes (e.g. high bytes as digits/space) was not exhaustively swept, though high bytes 0x80-0xFF in the port position all yield an invalid port.

Whether userinfo/query/fragment are stored verbatim cannot be confirmed directly (no accessor is printed); it is inferred from the fact that no other component is transformed and that removing them never perturbs scheme/host/port/path.
NUL bytes cannot be tested through argv, so behavior on embedded '\0' is unknown.
Length limits were not probed beyond ~120-byte inputs; a maximum-length cutoff in parse (as opposed to in the validators) would not have been detected. No evidence of one.
correctionsToEstablishedFacts: No established fact was contradicted. Two are worth restating more precisely: (a) 'http://[::1]:8080/x' is not an anomaly needing special-casing — host()=="[" and port()==-1 there, because the split is find(':') on "[::1]:8080" and '[' happens to be an accepted host byte; there is no IPv6 handling in the library at all. (b) 'query stripped before path' understates it: BOTH '#' and '?' are stripped from the whole input before the "://" scheme search, so a '#' or '?' occurring before "://" (e.g. 'ht#tp://x/y' => 1 0 0 0 1 [ht]) wipes out scheme, userinfo, host and port entirely.

Additional confirmation, not a correction: the leading hypothesis is_valid_url(u) == (!host.empty() || !path.empty()) held on ~11000 fuzz inputs with zero counterexamples, and 'a:///' => 1 while 'a://' => 0 shows the path retains its leading '/' (which is what makes ':///' and '/' report valid).
